https://www.politico.eu/article/france-d.text: French health authorities warned Friday that more than 40,000 noncompliant condoms have been sold online in recent months, urging anyone who used affected products to get tested for sexually transmitted infections. The products were “likely to pose serious risks to the health and safety of users,” including unwanted pregnancies and STIs, France’s consumer-fraud watchdog, the DGCCRF, and its general directorate for health, or DGS, warned Friday. Platforms selling the items were told to “immediately remove the ads,” with 36 listings taken down. Several sites have since promised to review their screening process. According to the statement, investigators uncovered around 30 condom lines that lacked the EU’s required CE safety marking and third-party conformity checks. Most were sold by Asian vendors through major online marketplaces. Advertisement Advertisement But the problem didn’t stop online. Tests of CE-marked condoms sold through shops and pharmacies found two faulty products — one carrying a “risk of bursting,” another with “the presence of perforations.” Recalls launched in May and August covered around 260,000 units. France’s warning follows a wider European crackdown: In July this year, the EU’s anti-fraud office traced more than 200,000 counterfeit condoms circulating under the logo of a well-known brand to a common source in China. Products were seized in Spain, Romania and Serbia. The French alert lands as STIs are surging across Europe . There were nearly 100,000 confirmed cases of gonorrhea in Europe in 2023, a 31 percent increase compared to 2022 and an increase of more than 300 percent compared to 2014, the European Centre for Disease Prevention and Control reported . It was the highest recorded rate in Europe since the ECDC started its surveillance of STIs in 2009.

https://www.dw.com/en/security-in-the-bl.text: Skip to content Skip to main menu Skip to more DW sites https://p.dw.com/p/5Nxgd A Bulgarian border police vessel carries crew members from a ship damaged in a drone attack on Tuesday Image: Petko Momchilov/REUTERS Advertisement Although security in the Baltic Sea and the threat of Russian provocation there are the subject of regular public debate, security in the Black Sea is a subject that sometimes gets less attention in the context of Russia's war in Ukraine even though the Black Sea is to a degree an active frontline in the war. There are multiple reasons why the Black Sea's security is such a complex issue, but two incidents in recent days have highlighted just how precarious the situation there is. On October 6, two cargo ships — the Alfa Watan and the Able — were struck by drones in the Bulgarian exclusive economic zone in the Black Sea. The Alfa Watan sank, and its crew has not been recovered. Bulgaria conducted a search and rescue operation, which was called off on Wednesday morning. The crew of the Able, which was damaged, was rescued by a passing Bulgarian ship. Two crew members were taken to the military hospital in Varna. Crew members from a ship damaged in a drone attack disembark from a Bulgarian border police vessel on Tuesday Image: Petko Momchilov/REUTERS The day before, another cargo ship — the Royad Mammadov — was struck by a drone and sank off the coast of Romania . Two crew members lost their lives. Multiple recent attacks on ships These are not isolated incidents. In the past few months there have been multiple attacks on cargo ships carrying grain from Ukraine . As a result, doubt is increasingly being cast on the belief that the western part of the Black Sea — the area off the coast of Bulgaria and Romania — is relatively safe. "Тhe Black Sea front is clearly expanding, and we should no longer look only to the Baltic Sea as a potential avenue for escalation and aggressive actions," said Ruslan Trad, global security expert and non-resident fellow at the Atlantic Council's Digital Forensic Research Lab. PM downplays drone attacks Bulgarian Prime Minister Rumen Radev downplayed the attack on the ships, remarking that ships are constantly being sunk in the Black Sea and that Tuesday's drone attacks were "probably not the most serious incident." Bulgaria's government called Tuesday's attack on the two vessels an "absolutely unacceptable violation of international law" but refrained from calling on Russia to end its war against Ukraine. Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy , on the other hand, was unequivocal. He said that the Ukrainian military had assured Bulgaria that it was not responsible for the attack and pointed the finger squarely at Russia . After a meeting of the National Security Council on Wednesday, a declaration was issued, which once again did not name the source of the threat in the Black Sea. Radev stated that the cargo and the direction of travel of the ships "logically speaking" provide grounds for a hypothesis pointing to Russia but stressed that there is no concrete evidence. He also contradicted Zelenskyy, saying no such conversation had taken place. Earlier he said that "if the war is not brought to an end in due time, it will continue to expand." Similarly, Bulgaria's Foreign Minister Velislava Petrova said that "we need to support all possible diplomatic efforts to bring this war to an end." Bulgarian PM Rumen Radev said that there is no concrete evidence that Russia was behind the attack Image: Spasiyana Sergieva/REUTERS The refusal to state clearly that it is Russian aggression that is putting the region at risk is not new for the Radev administration. Is Bulgaria a 'weak link' in European defense? For Rumena Filipova, chairperson of the Institute of Global Analytics, this is an example of how Bulgaria seems to be a weak link in Europe's defense against malicious influence from Russia and China. "This weakness stems from the lack of a serious institutional response to hybrid attacks of any kind, the absence of appropriate measures and a general tendency to downplay incidents," she told DW. "The perpetrator is not named explicitly, even though our partners in the European Union and NATO have already issued numerous warnings about what aggressive steps Russia could take against Europe," she said. According to Filipova, the Bulgarian government's narrative about peace without actually specifying the conditions or consequences for Ukrainian and European security is a demonstration of its leniency toward Moscow and raises the question of Sofia's geopolitical orientation . No smoking gun One of the surviving members of the Able's crew has said that he believes it was a Russian strike because the ship was carrying Ukrainian grain. The cargo vessel Able (pictured here in Istanbul, Turkey, on an unknown date), which was carrying Ukrainian grain, was damaged when hit by a drone on October 6 Image: Tony Hogwood/REUTERS Ruslan Trad says that the crew member's testimony is an eyewitness hypothesis, not hard proof. "The logic of motive, however, points toward Russia, as it is the state systematically threatening navigation to Ukrainian ports," he told DW, adding, "Until more concrete data is revealed the most accurate phrasing is 'probable but unproven Russian responsibility' without excluding other possibilities." Trad also pointed out that Bulgarian institutions lack experience in attributing maritime drones in Bulgaria's exclusive economic zone (EEZ). "When the system is uncertain, the safest institutional reaction is to say nothing until certainty is achieved," he said. "That is caution, but it is also a political choice." Economic consequences A direct military response or the triggering of NATO's Article 5 , which guarantees collective defense in the event of an attack on any member state, should not be expected. A marine drone, which Romanian Defense Minister Radu Miruta said was destroyed by F-16 fighter jets in August Image: Radu Miruta via Facebook/Handout/REUTERS Bulgaria's EEZ in the Black Sea is not Bulgarian sovereign territory and, as such, the strikes on the ships in this zone do not constitute a direct attack on Bulgaria — or on Romania in the case of the Royad Mammadov. Nevertheless, Ruslan Trad thinks these three incidents shatter the illusion that the western part of the Black Sea is a safe zone because of the distance between it and the frontlines in Ukraine. "This will increase pressure for tighter maritime monitoring, anti‑mining capabilities, coordination between coastal guard services and intelligence‑sharing among allies," he said. "The real effect will be a hardening of the shipping regime: stricter routing recommendations, higher insurance premiums and more difficulty hiring crews. Economic repercussions for local businesses can also be anticipated — imagine the impact on fishermen if they have to stay in ports constantly due to fear of further attacks. That is the intended effect of such strikes," he added. Rumena Filipova believes that although Romania, Bulgaria and Turkey strengthened their Mine Countermeasures Black Sea Task Group at this year's NATO summit in Ankara , this is not enough. She says there are far more substantial gaps in naval defense capabilities: "Modernization of Bulgaria's naval forces must be improved, much greater coordination — especially with Romania — is required. Yet, for more than a decade, Bulgarian authorities have downplayed or ignored the idea of developing joint naval defense forces and coordination, and that trend continues today," she said. Turkey's leverage and China's role Another question is how Turkey will react to recent developments. All three ships were owned by Turkish firms and some of the crew members were Turkish nationals. Turkish President Recep Tayyip Erdogan on Wednesday spoke to Russian President Vladimir Putin about the security of navigation in the Black Sea. Another cargo ship, the Royad Mammadov, was struck by a drone and sank off the coast of Romania on October 5. Pictured here: Firefighters and rescue workers wait to help the survivors Image: Romanian Interior Ministry/Handout/REUTERS Trad notes that Ankara has several levers of influence in the Black Sea: control of the Straits under the Montreux Convention, the largest fleet in the Black Sea and its role as a mediator between Moscow and Kyiv. "A realistic scenario is intensified diplomacy, coordination with Bucharest and Sofia, and pressure for safe navigation, probably within the existing trilateral anti‑mining cooperation. If it turns out that Turkish citizens were killed in a deliberate attack, Ankara's stance could become markedly tougher," he said. Filipova thinks that Black Sea security is already being perceived as a core issue — not only for the region but for NATO as a whole. In her view, there's not enough coordination between the countries in the region, which means that any response to threats does not come from a united front — something she feels has to change urgently. Filipova says that China's influence in the region and how it's connected with Russia is another factor. "We see not only the concrete military threat from Russia but also a subtler threat from China , which is less publicly discussed. But Beijing is trying to acquire strategic assets in ports, thereby gaining influence over both trade and critical infrastructure," she said. "Given that China and Russia cooperate closely, this constitutes a double threat for the Black Sea region." https://www.theguardian.com/australia-ne.text: ‘On what planet are you charging for a TV?’: Butler hits out at aged care providers The health minister has skewered aged care providers for charging residents extra fees for basic services like TV. Guardian Australia exposed the practice in July and recent ABC reporting has found new fee structure have made the problem worse. Mark Butler has told the ABC he discussed the issue with providers earlier this week. He said: I’ve been going to aged care facilities regularly since the early 1990s. TVs have been there for ever. Like, on what planet are you charging an extra service fee for a TV? It has been a basic entitlement for people in aged care facilities in their rooms as long as I can remember. … I do not consider TVs extra services. I made that really clear to them … I’m not going to sort of do a rule-in rule-out, but TVs are pretty basic … I think that [wifi] is too.
